That cash and goods were withheld to force assent is a characterization that needs a named source (e.g., MNHS).

citation: Blackfoot treaty Oct. 17, 1855; Royce 1899 Schedule; 11 Stat. 657, Art. 3; Royce 1899 p. 855 (remarks)

summary: Fort Laramie 1851 Art. 5 described a Blackfoot territory; whether any Blackfeet attended or signed was not checked (Kappler does not print the signatures). citation: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 14, 1865 (Little Arkansas); 14 Stat. 703, preamble, Art. VIII, signature block 707
quote: of the respective tribes not now present to unite with them and accede
summary: The treaty text recites that the signers were "duly authorized", but its own Art. 8 admits that parts of both tribes were "not now present". Six Cheyennes signed (four chiefs: Black Kettle, Seven Bulls, Little Robe, Black White Man; two headmen) and eight Arapahos. The Commissioner of Indian Affairs reported in 1866 that the Dog Soldiers "did not unite with their people in the treaty". That the commissioners told signers they signed only for their own bands, and the 8-of-280 lodge count, are Powell's accounts (not checked).

citation: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861 (Statutes at Large); 12 Stat. 1163, preamble and signatures
quote: Little Raven, Storm, Shave-Head, and Big Mouth, (on the part of the Arapahoes,) and Black Kettle, White Antelope, Lean Bear, Little Wolf, Tall Bear, and Left Hand, or Namos, (on the part of the Cheyennes,)
summary: The treaty was made by commissioners A. G. Boone and F. B. Culver, not by Boone alone. The four Arapaho marks were Little Raven, Storm, Shave-Head and Big Mouth, all Southern. No Northern Arapaho signed. A "Left Hand, or Namos" signed on the Cheyenne side; he is a Cheyenne, not the Arapaho Left Hand (Niwot), who did not sign. The same ten men signed the assent to the Senate amendment on Oct. 29, 1861. The text says the signers were "duly authorized" by the confederated tribes; the claim that they said they spoke only for their own bands is from Roberts 1984 and Fowler 2015, not the treaty.

summary: The US recognized the land between the North Platte and Arkansas as Cheyenne and Arapaho country. summary: Signed by survivors of Sand Creek (Nov. 29, 1864) less than a year after the massacre; Article 6 'repudiated' Sand Creek and promised reparations, while the treaty required the bands to give up their Colorado lands.

citation: Treaty of May 10, 1868, Art. 2; 15 Stat. 655; Kappler II 1012
quote: except the right to roam and hunt while game shall be found in sufficient quantities to justify the chase
